data.name: Tex Murphy: Mean Streets
data.detailed_description:
The year is 2033. Your name is Tex Murphy, Private Investigator in San Francisco. You've been hired by the beautiful daughter of a university professor to uncover the facts about his death. As you begin your investigation you uncover the deaths of several prominent members of the scientific community. Are these deaths coincidental or is there something more sinister going on?

And which characters could have a motive? Could it be J. Saint Gideon, former head of British Intelligence? Could Frank Schimming, president of the largest surveillance company in the world be hiding something? Or what about Sylvia, the professor's daughter. Is she as innocent as she seems? And why is an infamous Detroit hit man in town?

You'll interact with more than 27 digitized animated characters who respond to questions, bribes, and threats.

You'll rummage through offices, warehouses and factories looking for clues. With out innovative "tree" system you can search without typing.

Use your Lotus Speeder to fly to major cities along the West Coast. This land/air vehicle is a full 3-D solid fill flight simulator.

Stunning 256K VGA graphics combined with RealSound produce a software experience close to real life than has ever been achieved before. Some characters actually talk and respond to questions.

reviews.review:
Tex Murphy: Mean Streets is an unusually ambitious detective adventure that blends noir mystery, science fiction, exploration, interrogation, and even flight simulation into a single experience. Developed by Access Software and published on Steam by Nightdive Studios and Atari, it introduces private investigator Tex Murphy in a futuristic San Francisco where traditional hard-boiled detective fiction collides with dystopian technology. Its age is immediately apparent in its presentation and interface, but beneath those limitations is a surprisingly elaborate investigation that asks players to gather information rather than simply follow a predetermined trail of objectives.

The story takes place in 2033, with Tex hired by Sylvia Linsky to investigate the death of her father, a university professor. What initially looks like an isolated tragedy soon becomes considerably more suspicious when Tex discovers that other prominent members of the scientific community have also died. This turns the case into a broader conspiracy investigation involving powerful and potentially dangerous figures. Former intelligence officials, corporate executives, hired killers, scientists, and even Tex's own client become possible pieces of the mystery. The premise works particularly well because the game encourages suspicion rather than immediately identifying obvious heroes and villains.

Investigation forms the heart of the experience. Tex can interact with more than 27 digitized characters, questioning them about people and subjects connected to the case. Conversations can involve more aggressive approaches as well, including threats and bribery. Information obtained from one person can provide another name or clue worth pursuing elsewhere, producing a satisfying investigative chain. The game provides relatively little modern-style assistance, so remembering names and relationships becomes important. Keeping personal notes can make the experience considerably easier, especially once the number of suspects and leads begins expanding.

Environmental searching is another major component. Tex visits locations such as offices, warehouses, and factories while looking for evidence that might connect suspects to the deaths. The game's tree-based searching system was designed to simplify interaction without requiring players to type every command. Although this was convenient for its time, the overall interface now feels cumbersome compared with modern adventure games. Players must become accustomed to the game's logic and accept that some interactions are less intuitive than contemporary point-and-click design.

Perhaps the most distinctive mechanic is Tex's Lotus Speeder. Rather than treating transportation as a simple menu, the game includes a three-dimensional flight simulation that allows travel between major West Coast destinations. It is an extraordinarily ambitious addition for a detective adventure, although it is also one of the features most likely to divide modern players. The flight sections can interrupt the rhythm of investigating suspects and searching for clues, but they contribute greatly to the game's identity. Mean Streets feels like developers experimenting with how many different types of gameplay could exist within one adventure rather than following a rigid genre formula.

The audiovisual presentation is obviously primitive by current standards but remains historically interesting. Digitized animated characters, VGA-era visuals, speech, and RealSound technology were used to make conversations and environments feel more cinematic. Today the limited animation, low-resolution imagery, and basic sound can appear crude, yet they also give the game a distinctive atmosphere. The visual mixture of detective noir, early cyberpunk imagery, futuristic transportation, industrial locations, and digitized characters creates an unusual retro-futuristic character that complements the mystery.

Tex himself is an important reason the experience retains personality. He fits the familiar archetype of the determined private investigator operating in a morally questionable world, but placing that archetype within a technologically advanced dystopian setting makes the character more memorable. The narrative embraces pulp detective conventions rather than attempting to avoid them. Suspicious clients, dangerous criminals, powerful organizations, hidden motives, and conspiracy-driven science-fiction elements all contribute to the feeling of participating in an interactive detective serial.

The game's largest weakness is simply how much patience it demands from newcomers. Navigation, controls, searching, conversations, and flight mechanics come from a very different era of game design. There are few conveniences for players who become stuck, and progressing through the investigation sometimes requires careful attention to seemingly minor pieces of information. Players expecting streamlined puzzles, objective markers, extensive tutorials, or automated clue management may struggle. However, this lack of assistance also means solving a difficult portion of the investigation can feel genuinely rewarding.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than fully Verified. Core functionality is accessible with the default controller configuration, interface text is considered legible, and the default graphical setup performs appropriately. However, players may encounter non-Steam Deck button or input icons, the game does not properly support the Deck's native display resolution, and certain portions can benefit from having an external keyboard available. Considering its age and DOS-era design, it remains reasonably practical as a portable experience, but some control adjustment or tolerance for its older interface should be expected.

Ultimately, Tex Murphy: Mean Streets is more compelling for its ideas, atmosphere, and historical ambition than for mechanical refinement by modern standards. Its combination of detective work, character interrogation, clue hunting, science-fiction storytelling, exploration, and flight simulation remains unusual. Some mechanics have aged poorly, but the underlying mystery and investigative freedom still provide a rewarding experience for players willing to accommodate its vintage design. It is especially worthwhile for fans of classic adventure games, cyberpunk mysteries, detective fiction, and players interested in seeing the origins of one of computer gaming's distinctive private investigators.

Rating: 7/10
